ingredients.as_purchased_note: compounded powder or lump
ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian compounded-hing line, which is the product sold here (resin cut with wheat flour and gum). 4P+9F+4C gives 297, matching exactly. USDA has no entry, so there was nothing to cross-check against.
ingredients.notes: Pure resin would be far higher in gum and lower in starch; quantities used are a pinch, so the effect on a dish is negligible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: tin or packet of double-acting baking powder

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Leavening agents, baking powder, double-acting, sodium aluminum sulfate

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA double-acting baking powder. The carbohydrate is starch filler and the energy is negligible at the teaspoon quantities used; sodium is the figure worth carrying.
ingredients.notes: One teaspoon carries roughly 490 mg sodium. Consistency: 4/9/4 would give 111 kcal; the carbohydrate by difference is mostly bicarbonate and acid salts, which yield no energy, so USDA's 53 kcal stands.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: cut leaf sheet for wrapping or serving
ingredients.basis: Not a food. The leaf is a wrapper for lamprais, bath and steamed cakes, or a plate; none of it is eaten, so edible portion is zero and every nutrient is zero by definition rather than by measurement. No table entry needed or cited.
ingredients.notes: Carries no energy into a recipe; it is a packaging cost, not an ingredient cost, for the calorie side of the calculator.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: length of pseudostem, outer sheaths to be stripped
ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian banana stem entry, matched by the older plantain stem figure. Only the tender inner core is cooked, so less than half of a bought length is used, hence 0.45 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry basil (sabja) seed, packet

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Seeds, chia seeds, dried (nearest mucilaginous seed analogue)

ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian basil seed profile rather than chia, which is fattier; basil seed is lower in oil and higher in mucilage carbohydrate. Used a teaspoon at a time in falooda and cooling drinks, where the seed swells about tenfold in water but the dry weight is what is bought.
ingredients.notes: A large share of the carbohydrate is mucilage fibre, so 4/9/4 overstates energy by roughly 15 per cent.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: cleaned tripe, sold by weight

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Beef, variety meats and by-products, tripe, raw

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA raw beef tripe, matched within 6 per cent by the buffalo tripe entry. Babath is bought already scraped and cleaned, so edible portion is 1.0; it loses a great deal of weight in long boiling, which a cooked-yield factor should handle, not this row.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dried flowers, loose or in a packet
ingredients.basis: No food composition table carries dried Aegle marmelos flowers and I would not guess a proximate analysis for them. Left the nutrition null rather than invent it.
ingredients.notes: Used only as a steeped herbal tea; the flowers are strained out, so the brewed drink is effectively calorie-free and the missing values do not distort a recipe total.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet spice blend of coriander, cumin, pepper, cinnamon, clove, cardamom, mace and bay
ingredients.basis: No table covers packet biriyani masala, so it was modelled on USDA curry powder and checked against its distinctive components, cardamom and black pepper, which sit lower in fat; the chosen value stays near curry powder because coriander and cumin still dominate the blend. Held to low confidence because branded packets differ and some include salt.
ingredients.notes: Check the packet for added salt: salted blends can carry 3000 mg sodium or more per 100 g. Quantities are one to two tablespoons per dish.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: loose dry made tea, BOP or dust grade

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Beverages, tea, black, brewed, prepared with tap water

ingredients.basis: Dry-leaf composition estimated from the instant tea solids entry with the insoluble leaf fibre added back, because no table gives made tea leaf per 100 g. The number a recipe should use is the brewed one: about 1 kcal per 100 ml, since only a few per cent of the leaf dissolves and the leaf is discarded.
ingredients.notes: For calorie purposes treat a cup of plain tea as 2 kcal; the dry-leaf row is only for costing by weight.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled spirit, about 40 per cent alcohol by volume

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Alcoholic beverage, distilled, all (gin, rum, vodka, whiskey), 80 proof

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Alcoholic beverage, distilled, brandy, 80 proof (profile as distilled spirits)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA 80-proof distilled spirits; all the energy is ethanol, about 33 g per 100 g at 7 kcal per gram. Used in rich cake and Christmas puddings, where much of the alcohol bakes off but the energy largely stays.
ingredients.notes: 4/9/4 gives zero against 231 kcal; the gap is alcohol, as the brief allows.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry plain packet breadcrumbs
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA dry plain breadcrumbs. Crumbs made at home from stale local bread are drier than fresh bread but less dry than the packet product; the difference is within tolerance for a crumbing layer. Cup weight from USDA's grated-dry measure.
ingredients.notes: Cutlets and crumbed fish absorb frying oil, which dominates the energy of the finished dish.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet of sugar-preserved citrus peel, chopped
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA candied fruit, which is the same sugar-saturated preserve; the raw peel entry shows how much of the finished weight is added sucrose. Sri Lankan Christmas-cake peel is made the same way.
ingredients.notes: Used with chow chow preserve and dried fruit in rich cake; essentially a sugar carrier.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: sugar-preserved ash pumpkin pieces, sold by weight
ingredients.basis: Treated as a sugar preserve: the pumpkin flesh contributes almost nothing, and the syrup it takes up sets the energy at about 75 per cent sugar. Chosen between the candied-fruit and petha entries. Goes into Christmas cake and love cake by the tablespoon of chopped pieces.
ingredients.notes: No Sri Lankan table lists puhul dosi; the figure is inferred from comparable sugar preserves.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dried green pods
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA whole-pod cardamom unchanged; Sri Lankan cardamom is the same small green pod. 4P+9F+4C overshoots (377) because 28 g of the carbohydrate is fibre, which USDA does not count at 4 kcal.
ingredients.notes: Used in pod, clove and cinnamon quantities of 1 to 3 pods per curry, so the per-100 g figure rarely matters much.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: shelled raw kernels
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within a few percent; took USDA raw kernels. Cashew paste for a curry is the same kernel wet-ground, so the per-100 g figure carries over.
ingredients.notes: Sri Lankan recipes also use the immature soft kernel (kaju maluwa), which is far wetter and roughly a third of this energy.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry split dehusked chickpea

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Chickpeas (garbanzo beans, bengal gram), mature seeds, raw

ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian bengal gram dhal entry, which is the split dehusked form sold here; USDA's whole chickpea agrees within 2 per cent on energy but keeps the husk fibre. Dry weight basis.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: crushed dried red chilli, seeds in
ingredients.basis: The two tables differ by more than 15 percent on fat because cayenne powder is milled seed-heavy fruit while the Indian dried-chilli line is lower in oil. Sri Lankan flakes are crushed whole dried chilli with the seeds left in, so I sat between them at 13 g fat and 300 kcal. The 4P+9F+4C sum is high because 28 g of the carbohydrate is fibre.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled paste, salted, with some oil

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Sauce, chili, pepper, hot, immature green, canned

ingredients.basis: No table covers an oil-bound sambal paste. Built the figure from ground dried chilli plus the oil and salt a bottled or home-pounded sambal carries (roughly 8 g oil and 4.5 g salt per 100 g); 4P+9F+4C gives 128 against 130. The two USDA chilli sauces are thin, oil-free and much weaker, which is why they are quoted only as anchors.
ingredients.notes: Brands vary widely in oil and salt; sodium is the least certain figure here.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: ground dried red chilli, unsalted

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Sri Lankan chilli powder is plain ground dried red chilli with no salt or cumin, so USDA cayenne is the right match rather than USDA 'chili powder' blend (which carries about 1600 mg sodium). The Indian table is much lower in fat because it reports crude fibre separately and used older extraction methods; the value was set just under USDA cayenne.
ingredients.notes: kcal is consistent once the 28 g of fibre is treated as largely unavailable: 4P + 9F + 4(carb - fibre) is about 274.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled sweet chilli sauce
ingredients.basis: Sri Lankan bottled chilli sauce sits between a sriracha-style hot sauce and a Thai sweet chilli: sweeter and thicker than the first, less sugary than the second, so 105 kcal with 21 g sugar was chosen. Sodium set at 1100 mg, typical of the local bottled product.
ingredients.notes: Brands vary widely in sugar; a label reading should override this row where one is available.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet of dried agar strands or powder
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA dried agar for the strands as purchased. The figure overstates what the body absorbs: agar's carbohydrate is a gelling polysaccharide that is largely not metabolised, and USDA's fibre column understates that. A whole jelly uses only about 10 g, so the practical contribution is close to zero.
ingredients.notes: The energy in a china grass pudding comes from the sugar and milk, not the agar.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottle or packet of sugar-preserved chow chow (chayote), chopped
ingredients.basis: Read as the candied preserve used in Sri Lankan rich cake, not the fresh vegetable: chayote boiled in sugar syrup until saturated, so it was modelled on USDA candied fruit and set slightly lower at 300 kcal for retained moisture. The fresh chayote entry is given to show the gap.
ingredients.notes: If a recipe means fresh chow chow as a vegetable, use the chayote figure of about 19 kcal per 100 g instead. This ambiguity is the main risk in the entry.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried flower buds
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA ground cloves; whole and ground buds differ only in bulk density. Sri Lanka grows the same Syzygium aromaticum, so no local adjustment. Used in two- to five-bud quantities, so the piece weight matters more than the per-100 g figure.
ingredients.notes: One whole clove weighs about 0.07 g. Indian table consulted for agreement in order of magnitude only; its exact figures were not to hand, so no numbers are claimed for it.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: unsweetened cocoa powder, tin or packet

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Cocoa, dry powder, unsweetened, processed with alkali

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA unsweetened cocoa powder; the alkalised (Dutch) version is within 4 per cent, so either reading serves. Drinking-chocolate mixes with added sugar and milk solids are a different ingredient and run near 400 kcal.
ingredients.notes: 37 g of the carbohydrate is fibre, so 4/9/4 overstates the 228 kcal by roughly half; USDA's figure uses reduced factors.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: first squeeze of grated coconut, home pressed or a good tinned milk

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Nuts, coconut milk, raw (liquid expressed from grated meat and water)

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Nuts, coconut cream, raw (liquid expressed from grated meat)

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Thick first-squeeze milk, close to USDA raw coconut milk (230 kcal). The draft averaged thick and thin; thin milk is its own entry so a recipe's second squeeze is not counted at first-squeeze richness.
ingredients.notes: Thick first extract alone is roughly 300 to 330 kcal per 100 g; thin second extract roughly 100 kcal. Tinned coconut milk is comparable to the thick extract. Split the entry if recipes distinguish thick and thin.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: second and third squeeze of the same grated coconut with more water

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Nuts, coconut milk, raw (liquid expressed from grated meat and water)

ingredients.basis: A second squeeze carries roughly two fifths of the first squeeze's fat once the same flesh is pressed again with about twice the water; set at 95 kcal, between the MRI second-extract reading and household practice.
ingredients.notes: Recipe lines whose preparation says thin or second squeeze are pointed here by the draft normaliser.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: jar or sachet of instant coffee powder

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Beverages, coffee, brewed, prepared with tap water

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA instant coffee powder, since the entry is the soluble powder a household spoons into a cup; ground coffee (the alias) is mostly discarded as grounds and delivers about 2 kcal per 100 ml brewed.
ingredients.notes: One teaspoon of powder is about 7 kcal, so sugar and milk dominate a cup's calories.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: tin of sweetened condensed milk
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA; tinned sweetened condensed milk is a standardised product and local brands declare comparable values. Sinhala and Tamil household usage is the English brand name, so the script fields are left null rather than guessed.
ingredients.notes: A 390 g tin is the usual purchase unit.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet starch
ingredients.basis: Refined maize starch is the same product everywhere, so USDA was taken unchanged; the local packet labelled corn flour is this starch, not milled whole maize. 4P+9F+4C gives 367 against 381, the gap being moisture rounding.
ingredients.notes: If a recipe means milled maize meal rather than starch, protein is near 7 g and energy about 360 kcal.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole live or fresh lagoon crab, shell on
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA blue crab as the closest tabulated portunid to the Sri Lankan lagoon mud crab (Scylla serrata); both USDA crab entries agree within 2 percent. Edible portion 0.30 reflects heavy shell and claw waste on a whole crab.
ingredients.notes: One medium crab is about 400 g whole, yielding roughly 120 g of meat. Curry energy comes mostly from the coconut milk, not the crab.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: set curd in a clay pot
ingredients.basis: The two sources differ by almost double because USDA yogurt is cow milk at 3.3 percent fat while Sri Lankan mee kiri curd is set from buffalo milk at 7 to 8 percent. Followed the buffalo line. 4P+9F+4C gives 106 against 112.
ingredients.notes: Cow-milk curd or bottled yoghurt sold under the same alias is closer to 65 kcal and 3.5 g fat; thinned buttermilk (moru) is lower again.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: ground dry spice blend, packet or home-ground

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (NIN)
sources.entry: Coriander seeds (dominant ingredient of the blend)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA curry powder, which is a coriander-cumin-fenugreek-turmeric-chilli blend close to unroasted Sri Lankan thuna paha. No salt is added in the local blend, so the low USDA sodium is kept.
ingredients.notes: Carbohydrate is by difference and 53 g of it is fibre, so 4/9/4 on those numbers overshoots the 325 kcal by about 20 per cent; USDA applies reduced factors to spice fibre.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole, uncleaned
ingredients.basis: The market sells dallo as squid and cuttlefish interchangeably; took the squid line, which is the commoner buy and the richer of the two, and applied 0.70 edible for head, ink sac, pen and fins removed at cleaning. 4P+9F+4C gives 87 against 92.
ingredients.notes: True cuttlefish is leaner and yields less, nearer 0.60 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried dates with stone
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA deglet noor, which matches the ordinary pressed dates sold in Sri Lankan groceries and in Ramadan season; the stone is about 13 per cent of the whole date, hence 0.87 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh bunch of dill fronds
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA fresh dill weed, since recipes use the fronds; the seed entry is a different ingredient and is listed only to keep the two apart. Edible portion 0.80 after woody stalks are stripped.
ingredients.notes: Used in a few grams as a garnish for fish; contributes almost nothing to a dish's energy.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: curry cut, skin and bone in

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Duck, domesticated, meat and skin, raw

ingredients.basis: Sri Lankan duck curry is cooked skin on, so meat-only is too lean, but USDA's meat-and-skin figure is for a force-fed Pekin far fatter than a village or Jaffna duck. A value between the two, closer to the skin-on side, was chosen at 300 kcal with 27 g fat. Bone in a curry cut leaves about 0.62 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: small whole berries with calyx

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: No table covers the small bitter Solanum berries sold as elabatu, so the value was set from the two brinjal entries and lifted slightly for the firmer, more fibrous flesh and seed load. Edible portion 0.90 with only the calyx discarded.
ingredients.notes: Closely related thibbatu (Solanum torvum) is treated the same way. Berries weigh about 5 to 10 g each.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh roe sacs sold by weight

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Fish, caviar, black and red, granular

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA mixed-species raw roe, which fits the seer, tuna and sardine roe eaten here; the caviar entry is salted and cured and was used only as an upper bound.
ingredients.notes: Fat content rises sharply near spawning. Roe is usually fried or steamed with oil, which adds to the dish.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottle of liquid or powder colour, used by drops
ingredients.basis: No food composition table carries food colouring; permitted colours (tartrazine, sunset yellow and the like) are used at drops per dish and carry no usable energy, so all nutrients are set to zero. The alias saffron colouring is the same synthetic yellow, not saffron.
ingredients.notes: Treated as non-nutritive by convention. If a recipe means real saffron threads, that is a different ingredient.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole eel, to be skinned and gutted
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA mixed-species eel; the Indian entry is about 13 per cent leaner, within tolerance. Eel is one of the few oily freshwater fish eaten in Sri Lanka. Head, skin and viscera discarded give about 0.70 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: ground warm spice blend, packet

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Spices, cloves, ground; Spices, cinnamon, ground; Spices, cumin seed (blend components)

ingredients.basis: Computed as a blend of its components: cumin and cloves carry the fat, cinnamon and cardamom the carbohydrate and fibre, so it lands a little above curry powder in energy and slightly lower in protein. No table lists garam masala on its own. Used by the half teaspoon.
ingredients.notes: Blend composition varies by brand; the calorie effect on a dish is under 10 kcal, so the low confidence carries little weight.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: tinned or bottled clarified butter fat
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA anhydrous butter oil; the Indian table's 900 kcal assumes pure fat with no residual water. Both agree within 3 percent. Density given for melted ghee, measures for the soft solid as scooped.
ingredients.notes: Vegetable ghee (vanaspathi), sold as a cheaper substitute, is also about 900 kcal but is hydrogenated vegetable fat.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole brain, membrane on

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Lamb, variety meats and by-products, brain, raw

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Beef, variety meats and by-products, brain, raw

ingredients.basis: Goat brain is not tabulated; lamb brain is the closest small-ruminant match and was followed, with the beef entry as the upper bracket. Edible portion 0.95 after the membrane is peeled.
ingredients.notes: Very high in cholesterol (over 2000 mg per 100 g) and usually fried with oil, which the raw figure does not include.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet besan milled from dehusked chickpea
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA besan, which is the milled form sold here; the Indian whole-dhal entry is 8 percent lower, consistent with milling losses being small. Cup weight 92 g from USDA, as besan packs loosely.
ingredients.notes: Used for vadai and pakoda batter, where the frying oil carries most of the finished energy.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: petioles cut from the plant, skin on
ingredients.basis: No table carries Alocasia macrorrhizos petioles. Both aroid stem lines describe the same watery, faintly starchy tissue and differ by half, so I sat at the higher end at 20 kcal, closer to the Indian colocasia stem. Edible 0.70 for the fibrous skin peeled off. 4P+9F+4C gives 22 against 20.
ingredients.notes: Must be cooked with acid (goraka or lime) to break the oxalate crystals; nutrition is not the reason it is eaten.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dressed carcass, bone in

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Game meat, rabbit, domesticated, composite of cuts, raw

ingredients.basis: Followed the wild-rabbit line, since Sri Lankan hare is wild-caught and very lean. Edible 0.60 for a small bony carcass jointed for curry. 4P+9F+4C gives 108 against 114.
ingredients.notes: Only USDA game-meat lines exist for this; no Sri Lankan or Indian table entry was found.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bunch of leafy shoots with thorny stems to be stripped

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)
Indian Food Composition Tables 2017
sources.entry: Green leafy vegetables, group mean (as a cross-check)

ingredients.basis: Taken as a typical Sri Lankan mallum green: protein around 4.4 g, fat under 1 g, and energy near 50 kcal, the range the leafy group occupies in both the Sri Lankan and Indian tables. The exact Sri Lankan row for this species could not be verified, so the value is the group profile rather than a measurement. Leaves are stripped from woody thorny stems, hence 0.70 edible.
ingredients.notes: Eaten as mallum and valued as a galactagogue; its interest is minerals rather than calories.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: tub of vanilla ice cream
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA regular vanilla ice cream; the light entry shows the spread for lower-fat local products. Density 0.55 reflects the air whipped in, so a cup weighs only 132 g.
ingredients.notes: Used as an accompaniment (with watalappan or fruit salad) rather than a recipe ingredient; a scoop is about 60 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: small unwashed tubers sold by weight

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Chinese potato is not in the international tables. Published proximate analyses put the tuber near 70 to 75 percent moisture and 21 to 24 percent carbohydrate, drier and starchier than potato, so 95 kcal was chosen above the USDA potato anchor. Edible portion 0.85 after scrubbing and peeling.
ingredients.notes: Tubers are small, about 10 g each, and are usually boiled or tempered with coconut.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dried root pieces
ingredients.basis: No food composition table carries Hemidesmus indicus root, so the nutrition is left null instead of borrowing figures from another root.
ingredients.notes: Boiled to make a herbal drink and the root discarded, so the served drink is effectively calorie-free unless jaggery is added.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: brine-cured whole fish from the jaadi pot, to be rinsed

sources.name: Physicochemical and Microbial Characteristics of Selected Dried Fish Products in Sri Lankan Markets

ingredients.basis: Jaadi is salted wet-cured rather than sun dried, so it keeps much of its water and sits far below karawala in energy; protein near 22 g and fat near 9 g were taken from Sri Lankan market work on cured fish, and energy computed from them. Sodium set at 6000 mg because the fish is packed in 15 to 20 per cent salt; rinsing before cooking removes part of it. Head and bone removed give 0.70 edible.
ingredients.notes: Salt content depends entirely on the pot; treat the sodium as an order of magnitude, not a measurement.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: seeds saved from a jackfruit, white testa on
ingredients.basis: The two readings differ by about 16 percent on energy, mostly moisture in the fresh seed. Chose the middle at 165 kcal for seeds used straight out of a ripe or green jackfruit. Edible 0.70 for the leathery white testa and thin brown skin peeled off. 4P+9F+4C gives 169 against 165.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: roasted ground blend, packet or home-ground
ingredients.basis: Weighted blend of USDA curry powder and cayenne, because Jaffna powder carries a much larger share of dried chilli and roasted coriander than the generic blend, with a little less fenugreek. Roasting drives off water only, so dry-basis figures carry over. No salt in the blend.
ingredients.notes: No food composition table lists Jaffna curry powder; this is a computed blend, so it is set to medium. As with any spice blend, 4/9/4 overshoots the stated energy by about 18 per cent because most of the carbohydrate is fibre.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: solid block or moulded cake
ingredients.basis: Followed the cane-jaggery line and pulled it down slightly for kithul and palmyrah jaggery, which are softer and carry more moisture (about 8 to 10 percent) plus a little mineral matter, so they sit below refined sugar. 4P+9F+4C gives 356 against 355.
ingredients.notes: Kithul jaggery is stickier and a shade less sweet by weight than cane jaggery; palmyrah jaggery is close to the same figure.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled fruit jam
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA jams and preserves unchanged; a bottled local mixed-fruit or wood-apple jam is the same sugar-to-fruit build. 4P+9F+4C gives 277 against 278. No Asian table carries bottled jam.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh leaves, gathered rather than bought
ingredients.basis: No food composition table carries Macaranga peltata leaf, and I would not put a leafy-green average against it without a reading, so the nutrition is left null.
ingredients.notes: A piece is one leaf of about 5 g, used to wrap halapa.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole kidney, fat and membrane on

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Beef, variety meats and by-products, kidneys, raw

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Lamb, variety meats and by-products, kidneys, raw

ingredients.basis: The entry covers goat and beef kidney together, so the two USDA entries (which agree within 2 percent) were averaged; lamb stands in for goat. Edible portion 0.95 after the outer fat and membrane are stripped.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: one whole king coconut, water only

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: King coconut water is sweeter than the green coconut water USDA reports, so I followed the local line at about 5 g sugar and lowered protein to match. Edible 0.35 is the water drawn from a whole nut as bought (roughly 300 to 400 ml from a 1 kg nut). 4P+9F+4C gives 23 against 22.
ingredients.notes: piece_g is the water in one average nut, not the weight of the nut.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: tubers with skin and soil
ingredients.basis: Kiri ala is Xanthosoma sagittifolium, which is exactly the USDA tanier line, so I took that rather than the taro figure; the two agree on energy anyway. Edible 0.80 for peel and trimmed ends. 4P+9F+4C gives 104 against 98.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled syrup boiled down from kithul palm sap

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: No USDA entry exists for Caryota urens sap syrup. Treacle sold in Sri Lanka is boiled to roughly 70 to 75 percent total sugars at about 25 percent moisture, which puts it between maple syrup and molasses; 290 kcal with 72 g carbohydrate was chosen on that basis. Density 1.35 reflects the thick syrup sold by the bottle.
ingredients.notes: Adulteration with cane sugar syrup is common and would raise the sucrose share without changing energy much. Kithul jaggery (hakuru) is the dried form, roughly 380 kcal per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: young shoots and rhizome pieces, to be peeled and trimmed

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)
USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Taro, shoots, raw (related aroid, as a cross-check)

ingredients.basis: Kohila is a starchy aroid rhizome, so it sits far above a watery shoot such as taro stems; carbohydrate near 11 g and protein just over 2 g were taken, giving 56 kcal computed. The Sri Lankan row for the species could not be confirmed digit for digit, hence low confidence. Tough skin and fibrous ends are cut away, leaving about 0.75.
ingredients.notes: Kohila dalu (the shoots) are more tender and slightly lower in starch than the mature rhizome.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole-ground finger millet flour, packet
ingredients.basis: Averaged the two Indian entries, which agree closely; kurakkan is the same species and is milled whole in Sri Lanka, so the bran fibre and the high calcium stay in the flour. USDA has no finger millet entry (its millet is proso).

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh stalks, roots and dry outer leaves on
ingredients.basis: Only USDA carries lemongrass, so it was taken unchanged. Edible 0.55 for the tender lower stalk after the root plate and tough outer leaves are stripped. 4P+9F+4C gives 113 against 99; USDA reports no fibre split for this item, which explains most of the gap.
ingredients.notes: Bruised and simmered for aroma then discarded in most Sri Lankan curries, so little of the energy reaches the plate.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: trimmed slices sold by weight

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Beef, variety meats and by-products, liver, raw

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Lamb, variety meats and by-products, liver, raw

ingredients.basis: The entry covers beef and mutton liver alike, so the two USDA entries were averaged; they differ by 3 percent in energy. Sold already trimmed, so edible portion 1.0. The carbohydrate is glycogen.
ingredients.notes: Very high in vitamin A and iron, which a calorie table does not show.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole rhizome sections, skin on
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA lotus root; Nelumbo nucifera is the same species harvested from local tanks. Edible portion 0.80 after the skin is pared and the nodes trimmed.
ingredients.notes: Lotus stems (nelum dandu), used in mallum, are a different part and much lower in energy.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: tub or block table margarine, about 80 per cent fat

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Margarine, regular, 80% fat, composite, stick, with salt

ingredients.basis: Followed the 80 per cent fat margarine, which matches the table margarine sold in Sri Lanka for baking and bread; sodium rounded to 700 mg for the salted local product. A 60 per cent spread would be a third lighter, so recipes that name a brand spread should be flagged.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet
ingredients.basis: A Marie biscuit is a plain hard sweet biscuit, closest to the animal-cracker line and leaner than a butter cookie, so I followed the former and trimmed fat to 12 g. 4P+9F+4C gives 440, matching. The cup figure is for crushed biscuit used as a base.
ingredients.notes: Cup weight is crushed crumb, not whole biscuits. One biscuit is about 5 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: minced beef from the butcher, boneless

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Beef, ground, 85% lean meat / 15% fat, raw

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Beef, ground, 90% lean meat / 10% fat, raw

ingredients.basis: Set between the 85 and 90 per cent lean USDA grades, since a Sri Lankan butcher's mince is boneless trimmings at roughly 12 per cent fat, leaner than supermarket mince abroad. Used for cutlets, pastries and lamprais frikkadels.
ingredients.notes: If the recipe means minced mutton or chicken, fat falls to about 8 and 9 g respectively.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dehusked split green gram, dry
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within 1 percent; followed the Indian dhal entry for the dehusked split form, whose fibre is lower than the whole bean because the husk is removed.
ingredients.notes: Absorbs about 2.5 times its weight in water when cooked, so cooked dhal is roughly 100 kcal per 100 g before coconut milk.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: live, in the shell
ingredients.basis: The tropical green mussel eaten here is slightly leaner than the blue mussel, but the two sit within 16 percent and I kept the USDA figure for the fuller nutrient set. Edible 0.30 because meat is only a quarter to a third of shell-on weight. 4P+9F+4C gives 82 against 86.
ingredients.notes: Shell-on yield is the least certain number; small mussels can drop to 0.25.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled prepared mustard, or seed ground at home with vinegar
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA prepared mustard; a Sri Lankan mustard paste is ground seed let down with vinegar and salt, which lands in the same place. 4P+9F+4C gives 68 against 66. No Asian table carries prepared mustard.
ingredients.notes: Home-ground paste with no added water is stronger: closer to 150 kcal and 10 g fat per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried seed

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA yellow mustard seed; the Indian table for the brown seed used here is 6 percent higher in energy and higher in fat. Both are oil-rich seeds and agree within the 15 percent band, so USDA was kept for its complete fibre and sugar figures.
ingredients.notes: Tempering quantities are a teaspoon or less, about 18 kcal.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh whole berries

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: No USDA entry. Followed the Indian amla figure, trimmed to 50 kcal because the small wild Sri Lankan nelli is more acid and less sugary than the large cultivated Indian amla. Edible portion 0.85 for the stone and stem.
ingredients.notes: Local nelli berries weigh about 5 to 10 g each, far smaller than the 40 g Indian amla the source describes. Prized for vitamin C (several hundred mg per 100 g), which the energy figure does not capture.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried kernel or ground
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA ground nutmeg; the two tables agree on fat and differ about 10 per cent on energy. A Ceylon nutmeg kernel weighs about 5 g, and recipes use a pinch grated, so the high energy density matters little.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dried palmyrah seed-shoot flour, packet

sources.name: Comparative Analysis of the Proximate Composition of Palmyrah Pinattu and Flours (Odiyal, Boiled Odiyal)
IntechOpen, Scope and Nutritional Importance of Palmyrah (Borassus flabellifer L.)

ingredients.basis: Both studies put carbohydrate at about 77 g and fibre near 5.6 g; they disagree on protein (6.8 against 3.1), so 6.0 g was taken, nearer the study that measured the flour directly. Energy computed from the chosen macronutrients at 337 kcal, as neither source gives a usable energy figure.
ingredients.notes: Used for odiyal kool and pittu in the north; values are from research papers rather than a national table.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled sauce
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA ready-to-serve oyster sauce unchanged; the bottled product here is the same imported style. 4P+9F+4C gives 51, matching. No Sri Lankan or Indian table carries it.
ingredients.notes: Very high sodium: a tablespoon carries roughly 490 mg. Tamil script left null because there is no settled household spelling.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh leaves, sold in a small bundle

sources.name: Review of Pandanus amaryllifolius leaf composition (Trends in Food Science and Technology)
sources.entry: Pandan leaf powder, proximate composition, dry-weight basis

ingredients.basis: No national food composition table entry found for rampe. Took the published dry-leaf proximate analysis and recalculated to fresh weight at about 82 percent moisture; 4P+9F+4C gives 54 kcal against the 50 chosen.
ingredients.notes: Aromatic leaf simmered for flavour and lifted out before serving, so almost none of it is eaten; the energy it adds to a dish is negligible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet of dried uncooked wafers

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Derived rather than copied: an uncooked papadam is urad flour with salt and alkali dried to low moisture, so the macronutrients were taken from urad dhal and the sodium raised to about 2000 mg per 100 g for the salt and papad khar that the wafers carry. No table gives the Sri Lankan retail wafer directly.
ingredients.notes: Deep frying roughly doubles the energy of a wafer: a fried papadam of 8 g carries about 55 to 60 kcal against 29 kcal dry. Salt content is the main uncertainty.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: raw, in the shell
ingredients.basis: The two tables land on the same energy; took USDA kernels. Sold in the shell, and kernels are about 70 percent of in-shell weight, so 0.70 edible. 4P+9F+4C gives 610 against 567; the fibre and the shell-free rounding cover it.
ingredients.notes: Shelled or roasted salted peanuts are 1.0 edible and carry 300 to 400 mg sodium.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh or dried whole plant sold in small bundles

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Aerva lanata is not in any food composition table I could draw on, so the value is modelled on the range for Sri Lankan wild leafy greens (40 to 60 kcal per 100 g), using amaranth leaf as the anchor and allowing for the tougher, more fibrous stem. Marked low confidence.
ingredients.notes: Used as a medicinal decoction and in kola kenda, where the leaf is strained out or blended thin, so almost none of this energy reaches the bowl. Treat as a flavouring, not a nutrient source.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: block or slices

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Cheese, pasteurized process, American, without added vitamin D

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA processed cheese; the block and slice cheese sold here is the same pasteurised processed style rather than a ripened cheese. 4P+9F+4C gives 372 against 375. No Asian table carries it.
ingredients.notes: One slice is about 20 g and carries roughly 310 mg sodium.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet, seedless
ingredients.basis: Close agreement between tables; took USDA seedless raisins, which is what is imported and sold here as muddarappalam or sultanas. 4P+9F+4C gives 333 against 299, the usual dried-fruit rounding of sugars.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dried flowers, loose or in a packet
ingredients.basis: No food composition table carries dried Senna auriculata flowers, so the nutrition is left null rather than estimated from an unrelated flower.
ingredients.notes: Brewed as a tea and strained; the infusion carries no measurable energy.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet or home-roasted blend
ingredients.basis: No table carries a rasam blend. Computed it as a weighted mix of its parts, roughly coriander seed, cumin, black pepper, dried chilli and a little toor dhal, which puts it near 330 kcal with 12 g fat. The 4P+9F+4C sum runs high because 20 g of the carbohydrate is fibre.
ingredients.notes: Commercial packets vary in dhal and salt content; a salted blend can carry several hundred mg of sodium per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: milled white rice flour, packet
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA white rice flour. Roasted rice flour (the alias) loses only water on the pan, so the same dry-basis figures are used; hoppers and pittu are made from this flour.
ingredients.notes: If the recipe specifies red raw rice flour, protein and fibre run about 1 g higher.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: roasted split bengal gram, skinless

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Chickpeas (garbanzo beans, bengal gram), mature seeds, raw

ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian roasted bengal gram entry, which is exactly pottukkadalai, with protein eased down towards USDA. Roasting removes water only, so the dry basis holds; it is ground into sweets and thickenings rather than soaked.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dark-roasted blend of coriander, cumin, fennel, cinnamon, clove, cardamom, curry leaf and a little raw rice
ingredients.basis: No composition table covers the Sri Lankan dark-roasted blend, so USDA curry powder was followed and checked against its two dominant components, coriander and cumin, which bracket it. Roasting drives off a little moisture but does not change the macro picture at this precision. No salt assumed, as the blend is roasted and ground unsalted at home or by the mill.
ingredients.notes: Most of the carbohydrate is fibre, so metabolisable energy is well below 330 kcal; quantities per dish are small (one to two tablespoons). Consistency: 4P + 9F + 4C gives 398 kcal, but 45 g of the carbohydrate is fibre; valuing fibre at 2 kcal per g gives 308, close to the 330 chosen.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled distillate
ingredients.basis: A steam distillate: water plus trace aromatics, so it is effectively energy-free and no food table carries it. Set 2 kcal to stand for the trace soluble solids rather than claim a measured value.
ingredients.notes: The alias rose syrup is a different product entirely: sugar syrup at roughly 270 to 300 kcal and 70 g sugar per 100 g. If a recipe calls for syrup, do not use this line.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet blend of roasted coriander, chilli, fenugreek, pepper and a little toor or channa dhal
ingredients.basis: No table covers sambar powder. Modelled on USDA curry powder, with fat trimmed to 12 g because sambar blends carry ground dhal and less cumin. Low confidence: composition is brand-specific and some packets are salted.
ingredients.notes: Quantities are one to two tablespoons per pot of sambar, so the error contributes only a few kcal per serving. Consistency: fibre at 2 kcal per g gives exactly the 330 kcal chosen.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet of chicken or pork frankfurter-style sausages

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Sausage, chicken, beef, pork, skinless, smoked

ingredients.basis: Sri Lankan supermarket sausages are chicken-based and extended with starch and water, so they are leaner than the USDA beef frankfurter; 240 kcal with 18 g fat and 6 g starch was chosen to match declared values on local packs. Held to low confidence because brands differ widely.
ingredients.notes: Read the pack: meat content of local sausages ranges from about 40 to 70 percent, and sodium from 700 to 1200 mg per 100 g. One sausage is about 40 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet or loose, by weight
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree inside 3 percent; took USDA unenriched semolina, since local rulang is not fortified. 4P+9F+4C gives 351 against 360.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled cooking or gingelly oil
ingredients.basis: All refined oils are 100 g fat per 100 g; USDA's 884 kcal uses the measured Atwater factor for fat and is preferred to the rounded 900. Density 0.92 g/ml as for other vegetable oils.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried seed, unhulled

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA whole dried sesame; the Indian gingelly entry agrees on energy within 2 percent. Same crop grown and roasted locally for thala guli and thala bola.
ingredients.notes: Thala guli sweets combine this with jaggery, roughly doubling the carbohydrate share.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fermented salted shrimp paste block or jar

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Fish, anchovy, canned in oil, drained (salted cured analogue)

ingredients.basis: Followed the regional belacan figure for a salt-fermented shrimp paste: high protein, low fat, and salt at roughly 15 to 20 per cent, giving sodium in the thousands. Used a few grams at a time in sambols and Malay-Burgher dishes, so the sodium is what matters, not the energy.
ingredients.notes: Not in USDA or the Sri Lankan tables; the regional value could not be verified against a second independent analysis, so confidence is low.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled brewed soy sauce

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Soy sauce made from soy and wheat (shoyu)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA shoyu, the wheat-and-soy style sold in Sri Lankan groceries. Sodium is the number that matters for a household calculator and both USDA entries agree near 5500 mg per 100 g.
ingredients.notes: Sodium dominates: one tablespoon carries roughly 1000 mg. Locally blended sauces vary in added sugar and caramel.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry packet chunks of defatted textured soya protein
ingredients.basis: Textured chunks are extruded defatted soya, so the two USDA defatted-soya entries bracket it; 340 kcal with 50 g protein was chosen. Values are for the dry chunk as purchased, which roughly triples in weight when soaked, so a packet-weight calculation must use the dry figure.
ingredients.notes: Flavoured packets (the common Sri Lankan retail form) add salt and seasoning: check the sachet, which can push sodium past 1500 mg per 100 g. Soaked chunks are roughly 110 kcal per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole small gourds
ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian spine-gourd line, the same species; the USDA bitter-gourd entry is a different, much more watery fruit and is quoted only as a sanity check. Trimmed the Indian figure slightly to 45 kcal for the fresher, wetter local gourd. Edible 0.90 for stem ends. 4P+9F+4C gives 45, matching.
ingredients.notes: Tamil name left null; households know it by the Sinhala name. The two sources differ threefold because they are different species, which is why confidence is low.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: home-simmered chicken, beef or vegetable stock

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Soup, bouillon cubes and granules, dry, prepared with water

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA home-prepared chicken stock, since recipes here mean the strained bone liquid or the gravy from a roast. Sodium raised from USDA 143 mg to 250 mg because a Sri Lankan cook salts the pot; if a stock cube is used instead, energy falls to under 10 kcal per 100 ml and sodium rises above 900 mg.
ingredients.notes: Vegetable stock is leaner, about 15 kcal per 100 ml with almost no fat.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole corms with skin, sold by weight
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA taro, the starchier of the two readings, since Sri Lankan gahala and kiri ala are eaten as a starch staple; the Indian corm entry is about 13 per cent lower in energy. Peeled, hence 0.82 edible. Must be cooked, and the peel irritates bare hands.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fish, gutted and scaled
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within 3 percent; took USDA. Tank and reservoir tilapia is bought whole, and the flesh off a gutted fish is 55 to 60 percent of that weight, so 0.58 edible. 4P+9F+4C gives 95 against 96.
ingredients.notes: piece_g is one medium whole fish as bought.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fermented coconut or palmyrah sap, by the bottle

sources.name: IntechOpen, Scope and Nutritional Importance of Palmyrah (Borassus flabellifer L.)

ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian toddy entry with energy eased to 50 kcal per 100 ml. Fresh sap carries 12 to 15 per cent sugar; once fermented, most of it is ethanol at 4 to 6 per cent, so the residual sugar is low and most of the energy is alcohol. Used in hoppers as a raising agent, where a cup goes into a large batter.
ingredients.notes: 4/9/4 gives about 18 kcal against 50; the gap is ethanol. Strength and residual sugar vary widely by tapper and by hours since tapping.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled sauce
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA ketchup unmodified; Sri Lankan bottled tomato sauce is the same sugar-and-vinegar style product. Only USDA carries a line for it, so no second table was available. 4P+9F+4C gives 115 against 101, within the fibre and rounding allowance.
ingredients.notes: Local brands run a little sweeter and thinner; treat sugar as the variable figure.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry split pigeon pea, sold loose or packet

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Pigeon peas (red gram), mature seeds, raw

ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian red gram dhal entry, which is the split dehusked form used here, with USDA as a close check; the two agree within 3 per cent on energy. Dry weight basis, 200 g per cup.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: cleaned trotters, bone and skin in

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Pork, fresh, variety meats and by-products, feet, raw

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Lamb, variety meats and by-products, raw (for comparison)

ingredients.basis: No table carries goat or beef trotters. Used pork feet as the nearest analogue for skin, tendon and collagen, and pulled fat down to 10 g because goat and cattle feet are leaner. Edible 0.40 because most of the purchased weight is bone. 4P+9F+4C gives 178 against 180.
ingredients.notes: The protein is largely collagen, so it is not nutritionally equivalent to muscle meat. Long boiling transfers gelatine to the soup rather than leaving it in the meat.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dehusked split black gram, dry

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: USDA has no dehusked urad entry, so the Indian tables were followed; they agree within 2 percent. Sri Lankan ulundu is imported from the same South Indian crop. 4P + 9F + 4C gives 341 kcal, matching exactly.
ingredients.notes: Used dry in tempering (a teaspoon) and soaked for vadai or thosai batter, where it takes up roughly 2.5 times its weight in water.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet flour milled from dehusked dhal

sources.name: Indian Food Composition Tables 2017
sources.entry: Black gram, dhal (urad dal), dehusked and split

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Mungo beans (black gram), mature seeds, raw

ingredients.basis: Both tables agree closely; followed the dehusked dhal line because the flour is milled from split dehusked urad, which has less husk fibre than the whole bean. 4P+9F+4C gives 339 against 347.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: small bottle of vanilla essence or extract
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA vanilla extract. Most of the energy is ethanol (about 34 g per 100 g), which is why 4P + 9F + 4C comes to only 51 kcal; the brief allows for alcohol. The synthetic essence sold in Sri Lankan groceries is closer to the imitation entry, but a teaspoon in a whole cake makes the choice immaterial.
ingredients.notes: Used in teaspoon quantities; contributes about 12 kcal per teaspoon at most. 4/9/4 on the macronutrients gives 52 kcal against 288; the balance is ethanol.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: boneless deer meat in chunks

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Game meat, deer, loin, separable lean only, raw

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA game-meat deer; wild spotted deer eaten in Sri Lanka is similarly lean. Edible portion 0.90 for sinew and trim on meat bought in chunks.
ingredients.notes: Dried and cured venison (a common preparation) is far more concentrated, roughly 300 kcal per 100 g, and heavily salted.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry wheat vermicelli, packet
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA dry pasta for the dry-weight basis; Sri Lankan semiya is the same durum or maida extrusion, usually sold roasted, which changes water only. Cup measure 90 g for the loose roasted strands.
ingredients.notes: The Indian vermicelli figures are lower in protein because maida rather than durum is used; either way energy is within 6 per cent.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled white or coconut vinegar
ingredients.basis: Midway between USDA distilled and cider vinegar, because the bottled vinegar on Sri Lankan shelves is usually coconut or synthetic acetic acid with a trace of residual sugar. Energy comes from acetic acid, not from the macronutrients listed.
ingredients.notes: 4/9/4 on the macronutrients gives about 2 kcal against 19; the balance is acetic acid, as with alcohol.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bone-in cut from a dressed carcass

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Pork, fresh, loin, whole, separable lean only, raw

ingredients.basis: Took the wild-boar line unchanged; wild boar is much leaner than farmed pork, and the pork loin is quoted only to show the difference. Edible 0.70 for a bone-in jointed cut. 4P+9F+4C gives 116 against 122.
ingredients.notes: Fat varies a lot with season and animal; a fat-backed boar can run well above this.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled sauce
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA worcestershire sauce unchanged; the bottled product here is imported or licensed to the same formula. 4P+9F+4C gives 78, matching. Left both name scripts null because there is no settled Sinhala or Tamil spelling for the brand name.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: sachet of active dry or instant yeast

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Leavening agents, yeast, baker's, active dry

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA active dry yeast, which is what a Sri Lankan kitchen buys for bread and hoppers; the compressed-yeast entry is listed only to show the moisture difference. Quantities are 1 to 2 teaspoons, so the contribution is small.
ingredients.notes: Most of the carbohydrate is cell-wall fibre, so 4/9/4 overstates energy by about 20 per cent.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit with skin and stone
ingredients.basis: Followed the ASEAN reading for the species; USDA has no ambarella entry and mango is quoted only to place it. Edible 0.70 for the thin skin and the large fibrous stone. 4P+9F+4C gives 52 against 46, covered by the 2.2 g fibre.
ingredients.notes: Green unripe ambarella used for achcharu and sambol is more acidic and lower in sugar, nearer 6 g sugar per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole imported apple with core
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA apple with skin; apples here are imported and eaten with the skin. Core and stalk removed give 0.90 edible; a medium apple runs about 150 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dried split kernels sold by weight

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)
Published proximate analyses of areca nut (Areca catechu) kernel

ingredients.basis: Not a cooking ingredient and not in the major tables. Reported analyses of the dried kernel cluster around 8 to 12 percent fat, 4 to 6 percent protein and 50 to 65 percent carbohydrate with high tannin and fibre, which gives roughly 340 kcal per 100 g. Low confidence and no source values claimed, since I could not verify a specific table entry.
ingredients.notes: Chewed as a masticatory with betel, not swallowed as food, and classified as a human carcinogen. Included for price coverage; it should not feed a dietary calculation.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: green fruit with peel
ingredients.basis: The two differ by about 15 percent on starch; local ash plantain is a smaller, less dense cooking banana, so I sat between them at 115 kcal. Edible 0.70 for the thick green peel. 4P+9F+4C gives 123 against 115.
ingredients.notes: Starch converts to sugar as the fruit yellows; a part-ripe plantain reads sweeter and slightly lower in total starch.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole or cut piece with rind and seeds
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA waxgourd, the same Benincasa hispida sold here as puhul, with the Indian ash gourd entry as a check; both are very dilute. Thick rind and seed cavity discarded give 0.70 edible.
ingredients.notes: USDA lists 111 mg sodium for its waxgourd sample, which looks specific to that sample; 20 mg was used as the more typical figure for a fresh gourd. 4/9/4 gives 15 kcal against 13, the difference being almost all fibre.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit with skin and stone
ingredients.basis: Sri Lankan avocados are large, watery West Indian types closer to the USDA Florida entry than to Hass, so the value was set between the two at 140 kcal and 12 g fat. Edible portion 0.72 for skin and stone.
ingredients.notes: Fat content of local fruit varies widely by tree and season, so energy may range 110 to 160 kcal per 100 g. Usually eaten mashed with sugar or treacle, which adds to the total.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fish or cut steaks, bone in

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: The two agree within 7 percent; took the USDA skipjack line for the fuller nutrient set. Edible 0.60 for a whole fish cut into steaks with head, frame and skin removed at eating. 4P+9F+4C gives 97 against 103.
ingredients.notes: Fat rises in the season when the fish is in condition; kelawalla (yellowfin) is very close to these figures.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: ripe fruit with peel
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA banana with a small upward nudge, because Sri Lankan kolikuttu and rathkesel are denser and sweeter than the Cavendish USDA samples, while the Indian poovan figure of 116 kcal is higher than most local varieties. Peel is about 35 per cent of the fruit, hence 0.65 edible on a 100 g banana.
ingredients.notes: Ash plantain (alu kesel) used as a vegetable is a different ingredient: starchier, around 100 kcal, and cooked unripe.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: shelled fresh or frozen green peas

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Read 'batana' as green peas, the sense it carries in Sri Lankan produce lists (pattani in Tamil). Followed USDA green peas, nudged towards the Indian figure; the two differ by 13 percent, within tolerance. Edible portion 1.0 because peas are bought shelled or frozen.
ingredients.notes: If the priced item is dried peas (kadala batana), use about 341 kcal per 100 g with 25 g protein instead. Worth confirming against the price source's unit.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh pods, untopped
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree inside 10 percent; took USDA snap beans. Edible 0.92 for topping and tailing. 4P+9F+4C gives 37 against 31, covered by the 2.7 g fibre.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: curry cut, some bone in

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Beef, round, top round roast, separable lean only, trimmed to 0 inch fat, raw

ingredients.basis: Both cited lines are fully trimmed muscle, while Sri Lankan beef is sold roughly cut with visible fat and connective tissue left on, so I raised fat to 7 g and energy to 145 kcal and dropped protein a little. Edible 0.75 for the bone chips and gristle in a curry cut. 4P+9F+4C gives 143 against 145.
ingredients.notes: Local cattle are lean, so this sits well below Western marbled cuts; boneless stewing beef bought trimmed is closer to 1.0 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole roots, tops trimmed
ingredients.basis: The two tables agree on 43 kcal, so USDA was followed as given. Peeled and topped, hence 0.85 edible; a medium beet about 120 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit with core and seeds
ingredients.basis: Green capsicum is the common purchase, so USDA green sweet pepper was followed with a small allowance towards the riper red. Edible portion 0.82 for stalk, core and seeds. Script fields left as romanised for Sinhala, where households say 'bell pepper' or 'capsicum'.
ingredients.notes: Not to be confused with maalu miris (banana pepper), a hotter local chilli used in curries.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh leaves, sold in forties or by the bundle

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: The two tables agree; took the Indian line. Edible 0.95 for the stalk tip pinched off. 4P+9F+4C gives 44, matching exactly.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole bulbs with dry skin
ingredients.basis: Midway between the two tables, which differ by 25 per cent on energy because the Indian sample is drier. Big onions here are imported from India and Pakistan, so a value between the two suits. Papery skin and root plate discarded give 0.88 edible; one bulb 120 g as briefed.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fresh pods

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Took a value between the two tables at 20 kcal; the small dark Sri Lankan karawila is denser than the large pale Indian type but the absolute difference is a few kcal. Edible portion 0.85 for ends and mature seeds.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: white loaf
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree inside 3 percent; took USDA commercial white bread, which matches the standard Sri Lankan loaf. 4P+9F+4C gives 262 against 266. Cup weight is for fresh breadcrumb.
ingredients.notes: A slice of a local loaf is about 30 g. Sodium is the least stable figure across bakeries.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole or cut fruit with skin and core
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA breadfruit, matched within 7 per cent by the Indian entry. Del is eaten as a starch staple, boiled or as a curry. Skin, latex layer and core discarded give about 0.70 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit with calyx, sold by weight
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA eggplant, matched closely by the Indian brinjal entry. Only the calyx is trimmed, hence 0.92 edible; a Sri Lankan long brinjal runs about 90 g. Note that brinjal moju and fried wambatu absorb large amounts of oil, which the recipe must count separately.
ingredients.notes: 4/9/4 gives 29 kcal against 25, a 4 kcal gap from the 3 g of fibre.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole head with stalk
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA raw broccoli; it is an up-country introduced crop here with no local composition entry. Edible portion 0.75 after the thick lower stalk is trimmed.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: salted table butter in a block or tub
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA salted butter, since salted is what is sold here; the unsalted entry differs only in sodium (11 mg). Table butter is a standardised 80 percent fat product worldwide.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dried beans, loose or packet

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Lima beans, large, mature seeds, raw

ingredients.basis: Both tables agree inside 3 percent; took USDA large lima beans, which is what the market sells as butter beans. The 4P+9F+4C sum runs high because 19 g of the carbohydrate is fibre.
ingredients.notes: Site group is vegetable; pulse chosen from the brief's group list. Tinned butter beans in brine are a different line, roughly 115 kcal per 100 g drained with added sodium.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole head with outer leaves and core
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA cabbage, which the Indian entry matches within 8 per cent on energy. Up-country cabbage is bought as a whole head; bruised outer leaves and the hard core come off, giving 0.80 edible. A cup of shredded cabbage is about 90 g.
ingredients.notes: 4/9/4 gives 29 kcal against 25; the 2.5 g of fibre accounts for the 4 kcal gap.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole head or loose leaves

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: The two tables agree within 8 percent; took 26 kcal between them. Edible portion 0.80 after bruised outer leaves and the hard core are discarded. Cup weight for shredded cabbage from USDA.
ingredients.notes: An up-country head is about 900 g. Cabbage mallum adds grated coconut, which dominates the energy of the dish.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit with stem and core
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree; took USDA green sweet pepper, the usual local buy. Edible 0.82 for stem, core and seeds. 4P+9F+4C gives 24 against 20, within the fibre allowance.
ingredients.notes: Red and yellow capsicum are sweeter, nearer 30 kcal and 4 g sugar per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole roots, tops trimmed
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA carrot; the Indian entry is 17 per cent higher in energy, reflecting the sweeter red Indian carrot, while up-country Sri Lankan carrots are the orange European type USDA samples. Scraped and topped, hence 0.90 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole head with leaves and stalk

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA, which is within 17 percent of the Indian entry and gives the fuller fibre and sugar split. Edible portion 0.60 is low because the leaves and thick core are a large share of the purchased head.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: stalks with leaves, sold by the bunch
ingredients.basis: Close agreement; took USDA celery. Edible 0.92 for the root base trimmed off, counting the leaves as used, which Sri Lankan cooking does. 4P+9F+4C gives 16, matching.
ingredients.notes: One of the few vegetables with meaningful native sodium, at about 80 mg per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit, stems off

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Tomatoes, red, ripe, raw, year round average

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA ripe tomato and lifted sugar and energy a little, since cherry types carry more soluble solids than a field tomato. Edible 0.97 for calyx and stem scars. 4P+9F+4C gives 22 against 20.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: curry cut, skin and bone in

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Chicken, broilers or fryers, meat and skin, raw

ingredients.notes: Site group is meat; poultry chosen from the brief's group list. Skinless breast cooked for a diet dish is nearer 120 kcal and 2 g fat.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dry chickpeas with husk

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole head, leaves and stalks

ingredients.as_purchased_note: Ceylon cinnamon quills or ground bark
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA ground cinnamon. Ceylon cinnamon (Cinnamomum verum) differs from cassia chiefly in coumarin and essential-oil content, not in macronutrients. A 5 cm quill weighs about 2 g, which is how recipes here use it.
ingredients.notes: Two thirds of the carbohydrate is fibre, so metabolisable energy is far below 247 kcal; quantities are a gram or two per dish. Valuing the 53 g of fibre at 2 kcal per g gives 243 kcal, matching the 247 chosen; naive 4/9/4 would give 349.

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.notes: Corrected from the draft, which set an edible fraction of 0.45 against the whole nut while recipes weigh the flesh.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bottled white or virgin coconut oil
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA coconut oil at 862 kcal: the medium-chain fatty acids give slightly less energy per gram than long-chain oils, which is why it sits below the 884 of other oils and the rounded 900 of the Indian table. Density 0.92 g/ml; solid below about 25 C but measured the same.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried seed or ground powder
ingredients.basis: The two agree on energy within 4 percent; took USDA coriander seed. 4P+9F+4C overshoots badly (430) because 41.9 g of the 55 g carbohydrate is fibre, which contributes little energy. Sri Lankan use is dry-roasted seed, which changes weight by driving off moisture but not composition per gram materially.
ingredients.notes: Also the biggest single ingredient of Sri Lankan roasted curry powder, so this line drives that blend's figures.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh bunch with roots and thick stems

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA, which reports a higher moisture leaf than the Indian table; the gap exceeds 15 percent but the quantities used (a garnish handful) make it immaterial, and USDA's sugar and fibre split is complete. Edible portion 0.75 after roots and thick stems are trimmed.
ingredients.notes: A market bunch is about 40 g; a cup of chopped leaves about 16 g. Consistency: fibre at 2 kcal per g gives 22 kcal against the 23 chosen.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dry cowpea seeds

ingredients.notes: Grouped as a pulse rather than the grain label the price list uses.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fresh cucumber, skin on

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA with peel, since local cucumber is eaten skin and all in salads; the Indian entry agrees within a couple of kcal. Edible portion 0.95 for the ends.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dry seed, sold by weight
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA cumin seed, whose energy is within 5 per cent of the Indian table even though the fat splits differ; USDA's higher fat comes with lower carbohydrate, so the calorie figure is stable. Used by the teaspoon in tempering and in curry powder.
ingredients.notes: 4/9/4 gives 449 kcal against USDA's 375; USDA uses reduced factors for the fibre and the seed coat.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: sprigs, sold in a small bunch; a piece is one sprig of about 2 g

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Both tables give the same picture for a dry, leathery leaf; took the Indian figure. Edible 0.70 for leaflets stripped off the woody sprig. 4P+9F+4C gives 108, matching exactly.
ingredients.notes: Recipes count sprigs, so a piece is a sprig rather than a single leaf.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh immature pods
ingredients.basis: Both readings agree within 10 percent; took USDA for the immature pod, which is how dambala is eaten. Edible 0.95 for stem ends and any stringy edge trimmed. 4P+9F+4C gives 53 against 49.
ingredients.notes: Tamil script left null: Sri Lankan Tamil households use the Sinhala name or a regional one I could not confirm. Protein is high for a fresh vegetable, which is why dambala is treated as a substantial curry.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried red chillies with stalks
ingredients.basis: The two sources differ by more than 15 per cent on energy and by a factor of nearly three on fat, because USDA's cayenne is a fine powder with the oily seed ground in while the Indian entry is whole dry pods. A Sri Lankan household buys whole pods with seeds and grinds them, so a value between the two was taken, nearer the Indian entry. Stalks are pulled off, hence 0.90 edible.
ingredients.notes: One whole dried chilli weighs about 1.5 g; a level teaspoon of the ground powder about 2.5 g. 4/9/4 overshoots the chosen 280 kcal by about a fifth because 28 g of the carbohydrate is fibre.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: salted sun-dried pieces with skin and some bone

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh green pods sold in bundles

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.as_purchased_note: hen egg in the shell
ingredients.basis: Took USDA whole raw egg; the Indian value is higher because it is reported on a smaller, yolk-heavier egg. Shell is 11 to 12 percent of the purchased weight, hence 0.88 edible, and a Sri Lankan egg weighs about 55 g in the shell (roughly 48 g of egg). 4P+9F+4C gives 139 against 143.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole brinjal with calyx

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA raw eggplant; the Indian brinjal entry agrees on energy within 4 percent. Edible portion 0.90 with only the calyx and stalk removed.
ingredients.notes: Wambatu moju and fried brinjal soak up a great deal of oil: the cooked dish can be five to ten times this energy. Consistency: fibre at 2 kcal per g gives 23 kcal against the 25 chosen.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried seed
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA fennel seed; the same seed is used whole in tempering and ground into roasted curry powder here, so no local adjustment. Nearly four fifths of the carbohydrate is fibre, so metabolisable energy is much lower than 345 kcal.
ingredients.notes: Indian table consulted for agreement only; its exact figures were not to hand, so no numbers are claimed for it. Consistency: fibre at 2 kcal per g gives 327 kcal against the 345 chosen; naive 4/9/4 gives 407.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dry seed, sold by weight
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA fenugreek seed; the two tables agree on energy within 3 per cent. Fenugreek goes into fish and dhal curries by the teaspoon and swells but is eaten, so the whole seed basis is right.

ingredients.basis: The two agree inside 5 percent. Sri Lankan packet fresh milk is standardised near 3.8 to 4.0 percent fat, above the USDA 3.25 percent line, so I took the Indian fat figure and USDA sugars. 4P+9F+4C gives 67 against 66.
ingredients.notes: Powdered milk reconstituted to drinking strength lands in the same place; full-cream powder itself is about 496 kcal per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole bulbs with papery skin

ingredients.notes: Imported Chinese and Indian garlic have larger cloves and slightly better yield than small local bulbs.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh rhizome with skin
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA fresh ginger; the tables differ by about 18 per cent on energy because of the carbohydrate reading, but ginger enters a dish by the teaspoon of paste, so the difference is a couple of kilocalories. Skin scraped off gives 0.88 edible. Grouped as a spice, which is how it is used, though the price list calls it a vegetable.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dried blackened rind pieces, or bottled gorakka paste

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh green chillies with stalks
ingredients.basis: The tables differ by more than 15 per cent (40 against 29 kcal) because the USDA sample is a mature, sweeter chilli and the Indian one a young green pod. Sri Lankan green chillies are picked young, so a value between the two was taken. Stalk removed, hence 0.95 edible; one chilli 5 g as briefed.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit with skin

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dry mung beans with husk
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within 4 percent; took 344 kcal between them for the whole husked bean. Group set to pulse rather than the grain label on the site.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole head with outer leaves and core

ingredients.as_purchased_note: steak or chunk cuts with skin and centre bone

sources.name: Nutrient composition of 19 fish species from Sri Lanka

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole bulb with leaves and skin

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh pods with stalks

ingredients.as_purchased_note: loose leaf lettuce, bunch or head

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fresh limes sold by the piece or by weight
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA raw lime, which refers to the fruit without peel; the Indian acid-lime entry is the same species grown here and agrees within 7 percent. Edible portion 0.60 for peel and seeds discarded. Measures given as juice, since recipes call for spoons of juice or the juice of one lime.
ingredients.notes: One Sri Lankan lime of about 30 g yields roughly 15 to 20 ml of juice. Lime juice alone is about 25 kcal per 100 g. Consistency: 4/9/4 gives 47 kcal against 30. Much of the carbohydrate by difference in an acid citrus is citric acid, which yields less energy than sugar, and USDA's 30 kcal reflects that.

Edible portion 0.58 for head, gut, bone and fins on a small whole fish.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh yardlong bean pods

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh ridge gourd, skin on

ingredients.basis: USDA has no Luffa acutangula entry, so the Indian ridge gourd figure was followed and cross-checked against USDA calabash, another watery gourd; the two agree within 3 kcal. Edible portion 0.80 after the ridges are pared and the ends cut.
