sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Fish, cod, Atlantic, dried and salted

ingredients.basis: Took the Sri Lankan protein and fat figures for umbalakada (78.9 g protein, 1.6 g fat at about 12 per cent moisture) but recomputed energy, because the 180 kcal quoted alongside them is not consistent with that protein. 4x78 + 9x2.5 gives 334 kcal, in line with USDA dried salted cod scaled to tuna's higher protein. Sodium set at 1500 mg: umbalakada is brine-boiled and dried, saltier than fresh fish but far less salted than karawala.
ingredients.notes: Sodium is the weakest number here; it varies with the producer. Used in grams per dish, so its calorie effect is small.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole ripe fruit with skin and stone
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within 4 percent; took USDA ripe mango. Edible 0.65 for skin and stone on local varieties such as karthakolomban and villard. 4P+9F+4C gives 67 against 60.
ingredients.notes: Green mango for achcharu and curry is far lower in sugar, roughly 5 g per 100 g, and more acidic.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole tubers with skin
ingredients.basis: The two tables agree on energy within 2 per cent, so USDA was followed. Thick bark-like peel and the woody core discarded give 0.75 edible. Manioc must be boiled with the water discarded, which is a safety point, not a nutrition one.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet or tin of full cream milk powder

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Milk, dry, whole, without added vitamin D

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA dry whole milk; full cream milk powder is a standardised 26 percent fat product and the declared values on local tins (Anchor, Highland, Maliban) agree closely. Reconstituted at 12.5 g per 100 ml it gives ordinary whole milk at about 62 kcal.
ingredients.notes: The carbohydrate is lactose. Sri Lankan tea is made with this rather than liquid milk, so it is a real daily calorie source.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: sprigs with stems, sold by the bunch
ingredients.basis: Chose USDA spearmint over USDA peppermint (70 kcal) because the mint sold here as minchi or puthina is the spearmint type. The Indian line agrees on energy. Edible 0.60 for leaves picked off stems. 4P+9F+4C gives 53 against 44, the difference being the 6.8 g of fibre.
ingredients.notes: Site group is vegetable; herb chosen from the brief's group list.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: cut steaks, skinned

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: The two sit within 8 percent; took the USDA shark line for the fuller nutrient set. Edible 0.85 because mora is sold as skinned steaks with only a cartilage core to discard, so it yields far better than a whole finfish. 4P+9F+4C gives 125 against 130.
ingredients.notes: Shark carries urea that gives an ammonia note if not fresh; this does not change the composition figures.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bunch with stems, to be picked over

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Took the Indian ponnanganni macronutrients, which the Sri Lankan table tracks closely for the same species, and computed 48 kcal from them since neither source gives a usable energy figure. The thicker stems are pinched out for mallum, leaving about 0.70 of a bunch.
ingredients.notes: The point of this green is iron and calcium, not energy.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fish, gutted and headed at the stall

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA striped mullet; the lagoon mullet sold here is the same genus and a similarly moderate-fat fish. Edible portion 0.60 for a whole fish after head, gut, fins and bone.
ingredients.notes: Tamil name uncertain to me, so the script field is left null with the romanised form given.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried seed
ingredients.basis: The two agree on energy within 3 percent; took USDA. Sri Lankan cooking uses the small brown or black seed rather than the yellow one, but oil content is close. 4P+9F+4C gives 542 against 508, the difference being fibre and rounding.
ingredients.notes: Site group is other; spice chosen from the brief's group list. Seeds are tempered in oil and eaten whole, so the fat here does count.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: curry cut, bone in, some fat left on
ingredients.basis: Both reference entries are trimmed lean goat. Sri Lankan mutton is sold as a bone-in curry cut with visible fat and connective tissue left on, so fat was raised to about 6.8 g and energy to 140 kcal, above both tables; that is deliberate and is why confidence is medium. Bone and gristle discarded give 0.75 edible on purchased weight.
ingredients.notes: In Sri Lanka mutton means goat, not sheep. Sheep meat would be roughly twice the fat.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bunch of spring onion tops with bulbs

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Onions, spring or scallions (includes tops and bulb), raw

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA scallions including tops and bulb, which is how the bunch is sold and used; the Indian onion-stalk entry agrees within 10 per cent. Roots and yellowed tips discarded give 0.90 edible.
ingredients.notes: 4/9/4 gives 38 kcal against 32; the 2.6 g of fibre accounts for the gap.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit with peel

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within 2 percent; followed USDA. Edible portion 0.73 for peel, pith and seeds.
ingredients.notes: Local dodam (sweet orange, green-skinned) is more acid and slightly less sugary than the imported navel orange the tables describe; sugars may be a gram or two lower.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh clusters in a packet
ingredients.basis: Both readings agree within 10 percent; took USDA oyster mushroom. Edible 0.95 for the tough stem base trimmed off a cluster. 4P+9F+4C gives 41 against 33, covered by the 2.3 g fibre.
ingredients.notes: Site group is vegetable and kept, since the calculator treats it as a vegetable purchase.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole ripe fruit with skin and seeds
ingredients.basis: The two tables differ by about 30 per cent, the Indian sample being less ripe and more dilute. Sri Lankan red-fleshed papaya eaten ripe is closer to the USDA figure, which was followed. Skin and seed mass discarded give 0.70 edible.
ingredients.notes: Green papaya cooked as a curry is starchier and lower in sugar, about 35 kcal.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fish or steak cuts

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Read the label as paraw or paarai, the trevally sold on Sri Lankan stalls. No international entry exists for Caranx; local analyses of firm marine finfish give 21 to 22 g protein and 2 to 4 g fat, so 115 kcal was chosen, with USDA mullet as a same-order cross-check. Edible portion 0.60 for a whole fish.
ingredients.notes: If the stall means a steak cut rather than a whole fish, edible portion is closer to 0.85.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fish, gutted

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: The two readings agree within 5 percent for a lean white jack; took 105 kcal and 2 g fat. USDA has no trevally line. Edible 0.58 for a whole gutted fish cut into steaks, head and frame removed. 4P+9F+4C gives 104 against 105.
ingredients.notes: Trevally fat swings with size and season; a large paraw can read closer to 4 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit with rind; pulp and seeds spooned out
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA purple passion fruit, which the Indian entry supports within 8 per cent; the figures are for pulp with seeds, as a household spoons it out. Rind is about half the fruit, hence 0.50 edible on a 50 g fruit.
ingredients.notes: If the seeds are strained out for a cordial the fibre drops sharply and energy falls by about a third. Tamil script left null rather than guessed.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dried corns or ground, sold by weight
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA black pepper; Ceylon pepper is the same species and is sold dry, so no local adjustment. The Indian table runs higher on fat and energy, within the range explained by oleoresin content of the sample.
ingredients.notes: 4/9/4 on these numbers gives 327 kcal against the table's 251; 25 g of the carbohydrate is fibre, to which USDA applies reduced factors.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit with crown and skin

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA; the two tables agree within 8 percent. Edible portion 0.50 because crown, skin and core are half the purchased weight of a whole fruit.
ingredients.notes: Local Mauritius and Kew pineapples are sweeter than the tabulated average when fully ripe; sugars may run a gram or two higher.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole flower head with bracts

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Both tables agree; took the Indian banana-flower line. Edible 0.35 is the important number: the purple bracts and most of the stamens are stripped away and only the pale florets and heart are cooked. 4P+9F+4C gives 51, matching exactly.
ingredients.notes: Soaked in salted or turmeric water after chopping, which leaches a little of the mineral content.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: pieces of tender green jackfruit, skin on

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: The USDA entry is ripe jackfruit and is nearly twice the energy, so it was used only as an upper bound. Tender polos, picked before the sugars develop, follows the Indian tender-jack figure, raised slightly to 55 kcal for the firm Sri Lankan cooking stage. Edible portion 0.60 after the prickly skin and hard core are cut away.
ingredients.notes: Distinct from kos (mature jackfruit flesh, about 95 kcal) and from jackfruit seeds, which are starchy at about 130 kcal.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: curry cut with fat, some bone in

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Pork, fresh, loin, whole, separable lean and fat, raw

ingredients.basis: Set between the USDA loin (lean and fat) and the Indian meat-with-fat entry, because a Sri Lankan pork curry cut carries a visible fat layer and rind but is not as fat as the Indian sample. Bone and heavy gristle removed give 0.80 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: unwashed potatoes with skin

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: The Indian figure is 26 percent higher, reflecting a drier, starchier sample. Sri Lankan up-country potatoes sit between, so 80 kcal just above USDA was chosen. Edible portion 0.85 for peeling.
ingredients.notes: Potato curry and fried potato take up oil; the raw figure understates the dish.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole, head and shell on
ingredients.basis: The tables agree inside 13 percent; sat at 90 kcal between them. Prawns are bought head-on and shell-on, and the peeled tail is 50 to 58 percent of that weight, so 0.55 edible. 4P+9F+4C gives 89 against 90.
ingredients.notes: Site group is fish; seafood chosen from the brief's group list. Shelled, deveined prawns bought frozen are 1.0 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: cut piece or whole, skin and seeds in
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within 8 percent; took USDA. Edible 0.72 for the hard rind and the seed and fibre core, the seeds being roasted separately rather than cooked in the curry. 4P+9F+4C gives 31 against 26.
ingredients.notes: Sri Lankan wattakka is often cooked with the thin skin left on, which raises yield towards 0.85.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole white radish with tops trimmed
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA oriental (daikon) radish rather than the small red salad radish, because raabu here is the long white type; the Indian white radish entry agrees within 6 per cent. Peeled and topped, hence 0.85 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole head
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA red cabbage, which is denser and slightly sweeter than white cabbage (given alongside for comparison). Edible portion 0.80 for outer leaves and core. Used raw in salads here, so the raw figure is the one that applies.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry split dhal, loose or packet

sources.name: Indian Food Composition Tables 2017
sources.entry: Lentil, dhal (masur dal), dehusked and split

ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within 3 percent; took USDA lentils for the split red dhal that is the national staple pulse. 4P+9F+4C gives 358 against 352. Cooked dhal is about a third of this per 100 g because it takes up water roughly 2.5 times its dry weight.
ingredients.notes: Site group is grain; pulse chosen from the brief's group list.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: small red onions with dry skin
ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian small-onion entry, which is exactly the rathu loonu sold here; USDA's shallot is drier and 24 per cent higher in energy, and USDA's ordinary onion at 40 kcal is too dilute. The disagreement across sources is why this is medium. Skin and root plate on a small bulb waste more than on a big onion, hence 0.82.
ingredients.notes: One small onion is 8 to 10 g, so a recipe calling for ten is about 80 g as purchased.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: polished white raw rice, uncooked

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Rice, white, long-grain, regular, raw, unenriched

ingredients.basis: Keeri samba is a fine-grain polished raw rice, so the two milled white rice entries apply directly; they agree within 3 percent and 355 kcal was taken from the Indian figure, which better matches the higher protein of local samba. Cup weight 190 g as briefed.
ingredients.notes: Cooked rice absorbs about 2.2 times its dry weight in water, giving roughly 130 kcal per 100 g cooked.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry milled rice

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Kekulu red is unparboiled rice milled with part of the bran left on, so it sits between USDA brown rice and white rice. Followed the local red-rice line at 347 kcal with 2 g fat from the retained bran. 4P+9F+4C gives 344 against 347.
ingredients.notes: Cooked weight is roughly 2.5 times dry weight, so a cooked cup is near 140 kcal per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: milled white kekulu rice, loose or packet

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Rice, white, long-grain, regular, raw, unenriched

ingredients.basis: Average of the USDA and Indian milled white rice entries, which agree within 3 per cent. Kekulu is the everyday unparboiled white rice; the same row serves for nadu-milled white rice. Dry basis at 190 g per cup.
ingredients.notes: Tamil script left null: kekulu is a Sinhala varietal term, so only the romanised form is given.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: parboiled white or light red rice, uncooked
ingredients.basis: Nadu is the everyday parboiled rice, so parboiled entries were used rather than raw-milled ones; parboiling retains a little more fat and fibre from the bran layer. The two tables differ by 5 percent and 360 kcal was chosen between them.
ingredients.notes: Parboiled rice takes more water and longer to cook than keeri samba but lands at a similar cooked energy density.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry milled parboiled rice

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Rice, white, long-grain, parboiled, unenriched, dry

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Nadu is a parboiled medium grain, usually red-pericarp here, and carries a little more moisture and bran than the USDA parboiled white line, which is why it reads about 7 percent lower. Followed the local figure. 4P+9F+4C gives 349, matching.
ingredients.notes: Parboiling drives some B vitamins into the grain, so nadu is nutritionally a little better than white samba at similar energy.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: milled small-grain samba rice, packet
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA short-grain white rice, the nearest match for a small round samba grain, with the Indian milled-rice entry as a check; the two agree within 1 per cent on energy. Packs a little denser in the cup than long-grain, hence 195 g.
ingredients.notes: Parboiled samba would keep slightly more thiamine and fibre; energy is effectively the same.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: unpolished or lightly polished red rice, uncooked

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Local red kekulu keeps most of its bran, so USDA brown rice is the right analogue; energy was trimmed to 355 kcal because Sri Lankan red rice is usually lightly polished rather than fully unhusked, which removes a little of the germ oil. Fibre and fat sit above white rice, which is the point of the entry.
ingredients.notes: Traditional varieties (suwandel, pachchaperumal, madathawalu) differ in fibre but not materially in energy.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: milled unparboiled white rice, sold loose or packet

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Rice, white, long-grain, regular, raw, unenriched

ingredients.basis: Average of the USDA and Indian milled-rice entries, which agree within 3 per cent. Dry rice basis, 190 g per cup as briefed; cooked rice absorbs its own weight in water and lands near 130 kcal per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: dry milled rice

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: The two agree within 2 percent; followed the local samba line, whose slightly higher protein and fat reflect the short bold grain milled less aggressively than imported white rice. 4P+9F+4C gives 351 against 352.
ingredients.notes: Keeri samba and suduru samba differ mainly in grain size and cooking behaviour, not in these figures.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole long cucumber with skin
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA cucumber with peel, since salad cucumber is sliced skin on; the peeled entry is listed to show the small loss. Only the ends are cut, hence 0.97 edible; one fruit about 250 g.
ingredients.notes: 4/9/4 gives 18 kcal against 15, within the rounding of a food this dilute.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: lettuce head or loose salad leaves

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Lettuce, butterhead (includes boston and bibb types), raw

ingredients.basis: The site label covers whatever lettuce is on sale, so the two common USDA lettuce entries were averaged at 16 kcal. Edible portion 0.90 for bruised outer leaves and the core.
ingredients.notes: If the entry is meant to cover Sri Lankan gotukola or mukunuwenna salads, those are different foods at 60 to 70 kcal per 100 g. Consistency: fibre at 2 kcal per g gives 15 kcal against the 16 chosen.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: small whole fish sold by weight, ungutted

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)

ingredients.basis: Sardinella is not in USDA as a fresh fish. Local analyses of small pelagics put protein near 20 g and fat between 3 and 8 g depending on season, so 135 kcal was chosen below the fattier Atlantic herring. Edible portion 0.55 for head, gut and bone on a 30 g fish.
ingredients.notes: The cheapest fish on the stall and often cooked whole with bone, which raises the calcium contribution well above what this table shows.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet table or crystal salt
ingredients.basis: Followed USDA table salt. Energy is zero by definition and sodium is the stoichiometric 38.8 g per 100 g of sodium chloride, so no second table adds anything. A level teaspoon at 6 g carries about 2,325 mg sodium, the whole daily WHO limit.
ingredients.notes: Site group is other; condiment chosen from the brief's group list. Coarse crystal salt measures lighter by the spoon than fine table salt.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: bunch of leafy shoots with stems

sources.name: Sri Lanka Food Composition Tables (Medical Research Institute, Colombo)
Indian Food Composition Tables 2017
sources.entry: Green leafy vegetables, group mean (as a cross-check)

ingredients.basis: Treated as a succulent mallum green, a little lower in protein and energy than mukunuwenna because of its higher water content, and higher in sodium as succulents are. The species row could not be verified digit for digit, so the value is a group profile. Thicker stems discarded give 0.75 edible.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole long fruit, skin on

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: USDA has no Trichosanthes entry, so the Indian snake gourd figure was followed and checked against USDA calabash; the two agree within 4 kcal. Edible portion 0.85 after ends and the spongy seed core of an older fruit are removed.
ingredients.notes: Almost all of the energy in a pathola curry comes from the coconut milk and oil.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: leafy stems, sold by the bunch
ingredients.basis: Nivithi is Basella alba, not true spinach, so I used the vinespinach line rather than the Spinacia oleracea one (23 kcal, 2.9 g protein) to avoid overstating protein and iron. Edible 0.70 for the thick succulent stems trimmed. 4P+9F+4C gives 23 against 19, covered by the 2.1 g fibre.
ingredients.notes: Site group is vegetable; leafy chosen from the brief's group list. The mucilaginous stem thickens a mallum, so some households cook it in rather than trimming it, raising yield to 0.90.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole dried sprats, headless or with heads

sources.name: Tropical Agricultural Research and Extension, dried fish survey (Matara District, Sri Lanka)
sources.entry: Dried small pelagic fish, market samples

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Fish, herring, Atlantic, kippered (cured small pelagic analogue)

ingredients.basis: Dried sprats are a small oily pelagic dried whole, so protein near 57 g and fat near 11 g were taken from Sri Lankan dried-fish market work and energy computed at 340 kcal; the kippered herring entry shows the same fat level before drying. Sodium set at 2000 mg, lower than karawala because sprats are lightly salted. Eaten bones and all, hence 0.95 edible.
ingredients.notes: Calcium is very high because the whole fish is eaten. Frying sprats adds oil that must be counted separately.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole with roots and tops, sold by the bunch

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Onions, spring or scallions (includes tops and bulb), raw

sources.name: Indian Food Composition Tables 2017
sources.entry: Onion, spring, green leaves and bulb

ingredients.basis: Both tables agree; took USDA including tops, which is how it is cooked here. Edible 0.85 for the root plate and any wilted tops trimmed away. 4P+9F+4C gives 38 against 32, covered by the 2.6 g fibre.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: granulated refined cane sugar
ingredients.basis: Sucrose is sucrose; followed USDA. Measures set for level spoons of granulated sugar.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: cobs with husk; kernels are what a recipe uses

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA sweet corn; the Indian tender-maize entry is a starchier field corn harvested later and runs 45 percent higher, so it was not used. Edible portion 0.45 is kernels stripped from a cob bought with husk.
ingredients.notes: Boiled corn on the cob eaten as a snack is the usual form; the kernel figure applies to it.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: tubers with skin and soil
ingredients.basis: The two agree within 11 percent; took USDA raw sweet potato. Edible 0.85 for peel and trimmed ends. 4P+9F+4C gives 87 against 86.
ingredients.notes: Sugars rise on storage and again on cooking as starch converts, so a boiled bathala tastes and reads sweeter than this raw line.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: seedless pressed pulp block
ingredients.basis: Midpoint of USDA raw tamarind and the Indian pulp entry, closer to USDA. Grouped as a condiment rather than a fruit because the household buys a seedless block to sour curries. If pods are bought whole, edible portion drops to about 0.35 after shell and seed.
ingredients.notes: Only the squeezed juice usually enters the pot, but the pulp weight is what a recipe names, so per-100-g pulp is the right basis.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: small whole fruits with calyx

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Eggplant, raw (same genus, as the closest tabulated analogue)

ingredients.basis: No table lists Solanum violaceum. Set between cultivated brinjal and the related wild sundakkai, nearer the latter, because thalana batu is a small firm bitter fruit with more skin and seed per gram and therefore more fibre than brinjal. Calyx removed gives 0.92 edible; one fruit about 5 g.
ingredients.notes: Tamil script left null: sundakkai names a different species (thibbatu in Sinhala), so it would be the wrong name here. 4/9/4 gives 35 kcal against 30; the high fibre of a small seedy fruit accounts for the gap.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: steak cuts, skin and centre bone in

sources.name: Nutrient composition of 19 fish species from Sri Lanka
sources.entry: Lean marine finfish, raw muscle (species mean)

ingredients.basis: Sailfish has no entry of its own in USDA; swordfish is the nearest billfish but is markedly fattier. Sri Lankan work on local marine species puts lean white fish near 22 g protein and under 2 g fat, which matches thalapath's reputation as a dry, firm steak fish, so the leaner profile was chosen. Sold as steaks, so 0.85 edible; a whole gutted fish would be nearer 0.60.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh bunch with stems and roots

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: The two tables differ by nearly a factor of two on energy, a common spread for leafy greens sampled at different maturity. Took 32 kcal between them, since a Sri Lankan thampala bunch includes tender stems as well as leaf. Edible portion 0.70 after roots and woody stem bases are cut.
ingredients.notes: High in iron and calcium relative to its energy. Cooked as mallum with coconut, which supplies most of the calories.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: fresh berries on the calyx

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Eggplant, raw (as the nearest Solanum fruit)

ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian sundakkai line for the same species; the eggplant entry is quoted only to show that tibbatu is denser and more fibrous than a watery brinjal. Edible 0.95 for the calyx picked off. 4P+9F+4C gives 42 against 40, but the underlying reading is a single table, so confidence stays low.
ingredients.notes: Dried tibbatu, which some recipes call for, concentrates roughly fivefold and should not be costed or counted from this line.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: 425 g tin of mackerel in brine or tomato sauce; drained solids about 0.70 of net weight

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Fish, mackerel, jack, canned, drained solids

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central
sources.entry: Fish, sardine, Atlantic, canned in tomato sauce, drained solids with bone

ingredients.basis: Set between the two canned-mackerel and sardine readings, with a little carbohydrate added for the tomato sauce packs that dominate Sri Lankan shelves, and sodium at 500 mg for a brined product. Bones in a tin are edible and counted. Drained solids are about 70 per cent of net weight, which is the edible fraction of the tin.
ingredients.notes: If the recipe uses the sauce as well, the whole tin contents run nearer 130 kcal per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole ripe fruit

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Tomatoes, red, ripe, raw, year round average

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within 10 percent; took 19 kcal between them. Edible portion 0.95 for the calyx and any bruising.
ingredients.notes: A local tomato is about 100 g. Tomato paste and tinned tomato, sometimes substituted, are five to ten times more concentrated.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: ground dried rhizome, packet powder

sources.name: Nutritive Value of Indian Foods (National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad)

ingredients.basis: The two tables agree within 11 percent; took a value between them at 320 kcal. Used a quarter to a half teaspoon per curry, so the per-100 g figure barely moves a dish.
ingredients.notes: Fresh turmeric rhizome, sometimes used here, is about 90 kcal per 100 g.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: packet white flour
ingredients.basis: Both tables agree within 5 percent; took USDA unenriched all-purpose flour, since local packet flour is not fortified the way US flour is. 4P+9F+4C gives 355 against 364. Site group grain replaced with flour from the brief's list.
ingredients.notes: Atta or wholemeal flour is a separate line: about 340 kcal with 11 g fibre.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit in its hard shell
ingredients.basis: Followed the Indian wood apple entry, confirmed by the newer table; the unusually high protein and fat for a fruit come from the seeds embedded in the pulp, which are eaten with it. The hard shell is about half the fruit, hence 0.50 edible. Diwul is beaten with jaggery and coconut milk, so the added sugar dominates a serving.
ingredients.notes: No USDA entry exists for this fruit, so both sources are Indian.

ingredients.as_purchased_note: whole fruit, skin on

sources.name: USDA FoodData Central (SR Legacy)
sources.entry: Squash, summer, zucchini, includes skin, raw

ingredients.basis: Followed USDA zucchini with skin; the general summer squash entry agrees within 1 kcal. An introduced crop with no local table entry and no settled Sinhala or Tamil name, so both script fields are left null with the English romanisation.
